t: How To Be The Teacher Your Students Need
q: Her classroom was chaotic. Her students played and goofed off. They yelled and roughhoused.
Because, you see, she was paralyzed by fear. She was afraid that if she held her students to a standard of behavior that was required for success in school, then they would rebel.
Consistent accountability is the foundation upon which trust, likability, and influence are built.

My advice to the teacher I observed that day is to take ‘you’ out of the equation. Turn down the volume on how you feel—your thoughts, worries, anxieties, and what ifs—and turn up the volume on how urgently your students need you.
So when you freeze up, when you look the other way, when you bribe and appease and give up and give in, you set them up for failure and crushing disappointment.
Your students need a rescuer, a defender, a role model, a lion, and a champion. They need a hero who will make a stand for them and their future.
This is your chosen career, after all, and you have but one chance to make an impact on each student that comes into your life. One opportunity. Don’t waste it.
x: Knowing the strategies of good classroom management is not enough; fear of student rebellion often prevents teachers from applying them.
Shifting focus from personal anxiety to how urgently students depend on their teacher can dissolve paralyzing fear.
Consistent accountability, not avoidance, is what builds the trust, respect, and leverage that make effective teaching possible.

Fear-driven inaction — looking the other way, bribing, giving up — sets students up for real failure later in life.

t: How To Handle Students Who Dominate Discussions ussions/
q: Because it’s a clear sign that a majority of your students don’t feel safe enough to participate.
But this is a misguided approach and a detriment to your classroom. Because those few students are doing nothing wrong. In fact, they can serve as role models for the rest of the class.
Class-wide participation is a function of how well you protect your students from interruption—and not just during discussions, but all the time.
The upshot is that to improve participation class wide, you must first convince your students that they can voice their deepest thoughts and opinions without being interrupted.
It’s important to point out that this feeling of security is a prerequisite only—the critical first step.
They focus their attention on making their lessons more interesting—often under the advisement of a well-meaning administrator—yet neglect the one thing that students need first and foremost: Safety.
Make your students feel safe to take chances, step out of their comfort zone, and contribute their innermost point of view. And they will.
x: A few students dominating discussion is not itself the problem — it signals that the rest of the class doesn't feel safe enough to participate.
Vocal students shouldn't be tamped down; they can serve as role models and are simply filling a void others aren't filling.
Class-wide participation depends on consistent protection from interruption throughout the entire day, not just during discussions.
Psychological safety, not more engaging lesson content, must come first — many teachers have this sequence backwards.
Linsin reframes the common problem of a few students dominating discussions while the rest stay silent, arguing that the outspoken few are not the problem and shouldn't be tamped down.

Linsin also pushes back on the common instinct to focus first on making lessons more engaging, arguing that safety must come before compelling content, since many teachers have the sequence backwards.
The article closes with a direct charge: make students feel safe to take risks, and participation will follow.

t: One Of The Worst Classroom Management Strategies I've Ever Seen trategies-ive-ever-seen/
q: I won't mention the program by name, but at its core, it's a token economy, whereby students are rewarded in exchange for 'good' (i.e. expected) behavior.
Worst of all, though, token economies snuff out intrinsic motivation.
In other words, you would ignore the misbehaving student, but effusively inform those in proximity how wonderful they are for doing what they're supposed to do.
It’s also cruel and demeaning and, in this case, uses well-behaved students as pawns to elicit compliant behavior from the misbehaving student.
That this method is endorsed, taught, and even promoted in school districts around the country is tragic and shameful.
Praise only what is praiseworthy. Look for legitimate improvement, new learning, or greater effort than they’ve given before, and then let them know you notice.

This way, your words of praise will mean something to them, firing their intrinsic motivational engines deep within their heart. They’ll know that if you said it, it must be true. And the truth will set them free.
x: After observing a training on a popular token-economy program, Linsin revisits his long-standing criticism of rewarding students for expected behavior, arguing such systems encourage cheating, weaken relationships, and…
Token economies encourage cheating and stealing, weaken the student-teacher relationship, and undermine intrinsic motivation.
This tactic offers the misbehaving student no genuine feedback they can use to actually improve their behavior.
The "caught being good" tactic — praising well-behaved neighbors while ignoring a misbehaving student — is dishonest and uses other students as pawns.
